Unsupervised Pitfalls

  • No ground truth
    • How many dimensions are right?
    • How many clusters?
  • No accuracy, training sets, testing sets, cross-validation, etc

Consequences

  • Choices are modeling decisions
    • You have to choose based on usefulness and your knowledge
    • Level of trust is lower
  • Promulgamation of algorithms

Principal Component Analysis (PCA)

  • Goal of PCA is to find a small set of features which explain most of the variability in the dataset
  • New directions called Principal Components

Principal Components

  • Each PC is a linear combination of original features: \[ Z_1 = \phi_{11}X_1 + \phi_{21}X_2 + \cdots + \phi_{p1}X_p \]

Principal Components

  • Each PC is a linear combination of original features:

\[ \begin{aligned} Z_1 &= \phi_{11}X_1 + \phi_{21}X_2 + \cdots + \phi_{p1}X_p \\ Z_2 &= \phi_{12}X_1 + \phi_{22}X_2 + \cdots + \phi_{p2}X_p \\ &\;\;\vdots \\ Z_p &= \phi_{1p}X_1 + \phi_{2p}X_2 + \cdots + \phi_{pp}X_p \end{aligned} \]

Loadings

  • \(\phi\) terms are called loadings
  • \(\phi\) are normalized: \[ \phi_{1j}^2+\phi_{2j}^2+\cdots+\phi_{pj}^2 = \sum_{i=1}^p \phi_{ij}^2 = \|\boldsymbol{\phi}_j\|^2 = 1 \]
  • Can write it as a loading matrix \(\Phi\)
  • \(\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{X}\mathbf{\Phi}\)

Linearly Independent PCs

  • Principal Components are linearly independent

Principal Component Algorithm

  • First PC explains as much variance of your dataset as possible
  • Second PC explains as much of remaining variance as possible
  • Third PC explains as much of remaining variance as possible
  • etc

PCA Algo

  • Make a “1D” dataset in two dimensions
  • Data lies along a straight line with some noise

Simple PCA Example

  • PCA looks for vectors along which the “variance” is maximized

Simple PCA Example

  • Project data points onto component

Find the Variance

  • Project data points onto component

Looking at Multiple Projections

  • Any projection is possible

First Principal Component

  • PC1 maximizes variance

Continue Process to find PCs

  • PC1 is the direction with the most variance
  • PC2 is perpendicular to PC1, most variance
  • PC3 is perpendicular to PC1 and PC2, most variance
  • \(P\) dimensional dataset has \(P\) PCs

Linear Algebra (DATA 605) Explanation

  • PCs are right singular vectors of Data Matrix
  • Variance explained proportional to squres of singular values \[ \mathbf{X} = \mathbf{U} \mathbf{\Sigma} \mathbf{V}^T \]

Alternative Explanation

  • Suppose we want to find best \(d\) dimensional coordinates to describe our data set?
  • First \(d\) principal components are the coordinates

  • Suppose we want to find best \(d\) dimensional coordinates to describe our data set?
  • First \(d\) principal components are the coordinates

Normalization

Normalization

  • Standard Advice:
    • Scale to mean 0 and unit variance for each feature

Normalization

  • PCs much more informative if we transform to per capita variables first

Other Normalization Considerations

  • If you think natural variance has information
    • Quantities have same units
    • There is a known measurement error
    • Extensive versus intensive variables
    • ‘log’ transform

Which PCs are meaningful?

  • Heuristic Method:
    • Look at first few principal components
    • If they show an interesting pattern, look at next few
    • Repat until it stops

Which PCs are meaningful?

  • Elbow of scree plot
  • You can discard low variance PCs

Picking a Dimension

  • You can discard low variance PCs
  • Use “Elbow” of plot to pick cutoff

Random Matrix Theory

  • Permute columns randomly and compare explained variance
  • Marchenko-Pastur distribution: \(\sqrt{p}-\sqrt{n}\) and \(\sqrt{p}+\sqrt{n}\)

PCA in Supervised Learning

  • Can use PCA to generate features for supervised learning
  • Predict cancer from the 4000 biomarkers: logistic regression on the first \(M\) PCs, choose \(M\) by 10-fold CV
pcr = Pipeline([("scaler", StandardScaler()),
                ("pca", PCA()),
                ("logreg", LogisticRegression(max_iter=5000))])

components_tried = list(range(1, 21)) + [30, 50, 100]
pcr_search = GridSearchCV(pcr,
                          {"pca__n_components": components_tried},
                          cv=StratifiedKFold(n_splits=10, shuffle=True, random_state=0),
                          scoring="neg_log_loss")
pcr_search.fit(ovarian_features, ovarian_status["status"] == "Cancer")

CV Error by Number of Components

PCA in sklearn

  • StandardScaler centers and normalizes
  • PCA calculates components
  • transform calculates embeddings
ovarian_scaled = StandardScaler().fit_transform(ovarian_features)
ovarian_pca = PCA().fit(ovarian_scaled)
ovarian_scores = ovarian_pca.transform(ovarian_scaled)

Hard-Impute

  • Can use PCA to impute missing (at random) values
  • Step 1: Impute using mean
  • Step 2: Calculate ‘M’ dimensional embedding of imputed data using PCA
  • Step 3: Replace mean imputed values with their ‘M’ dimensional embedding value
  • Step 4: Evaluate error on observations wrt to embedding
  • Step 5: Repeat 2-4, stop when error flattens

Hard-Impute

  • Here we randomly delete 10% of observations and impute

Impute on Residuals

  • Fit a basic model: \[ \hat{r}_{ui} = \mu + b_u + b_i \]
  • Calculate residual matrix: \[ \delta_{ui} = r_{ui} - \hat{r}_{ui} \]
  • Do matrix completion to get residuals

Downsides of PCA

  • Sensitive to outliers
    • If your measurement process is not robust….
    • Using PCA could be very misleading!
  • There is an algorithm called robust PCA which is great these cases

Outliers Break PCA

  • Add three outliers to the Ovarian Cancer dataset

Robust PCA: Principal Component Pursuit

  • Split \(X = L + S\) into a low rank part and a sparse part: minimize \(\|L\|_* + \lambda \|S\|_1\) with \(\lambda = 1/\sqrt{\max(n, p)}\)
  • skpcp implements this, need to choose some hyperparameters including ‘max_iter’
from skpcp import PCP

pcp_model = PCP(max_iter=300).fit(ovarian_corrupted)
ovarian_low_rank = pcp_model.low_rank_

Robust PCA: Principal Component Pursuit

Clustering

  • Clustering involves discovering labels that group nearby points into categories in an unlabelled dataset
  • Need a distance metric and a choice for number of clusters

Clustering Application: Weather Regimes

  • Cluster daily winter pressure maps over the North Atlantic: four recurring patterns explain European weather
  • Atlantic Ridge, Scandinavian Blocking, and the two phases of the North Atlantic Oscillation

Falkena, de Wiljes, Weisheimer, and Shepherd (2020), Q. J. R. Meteorol. Soc. 146, 2801–2814, Figure 5. CC BY 4.0.

Clustering Application: Customer Segmentation

  • Group shoppers by income and spending to target each segment differently

Clustering Application: Anomaly Detection

  • Learn what normal network traffic looks like
  • Look for points far from clusters: KDD Cup 1999

Clustering Application: Study Design

  • NEON, the national ecological observatory, clustered the US into ecoclimatic regions with k-means
  • One core field site represents each of the 20 domains

k-means method

  • Most common clustering method
  • Needs two things:
    • Measure of distance between points
    • Number of Clusters to find
  • Each cluster characterized by a center
  • Points clustered to closest center

K-Means Clustering

  • Choose the number of clusters \(K\) in advance
  • Find clusters \(C_1, \dots, C_K\) with means \(\mu_1, \dots, \mu_K\) that minimize the within-cluster sum of squares: \[ W = \sum_{k=1}^K \sum_{i \in C_k} \|x_i - \mu_k\|^2 \]
  • Finding the exact minimum is computationally intractable, so we search for a good local minimum

K-Means Algorithm

  1. Start with \(K\) means, often \(K\) randomly chosen data points
  2. Assign each point to its nearest mean
  3. Move each mean to the average of the points assigned to it
  4. Repeat 2 and 3 until nothing changes
  • Steps 2 and 3 can only lower \(W\), so the algorithm always converges
  • It converges to a local minimum that depends on where it started

K-Means in Action

  • Ruspini 4 Cluster Example

Starting Points Matter

  • Same data, different random starting points

Starting Points Matter

  • Same data, different random starting points

Convergence

  • \(W\) falls at every step, then stops at a local minimum

K-Means in sklearn

ruspini_kmeans = KMeans(n_clusters=4, n_init=10, random_state=1).fit(ruspini)

ruspini_kmeans.labels_[:10], ruspini_kmeans.cluster_centers_.round(1), round(ruspini_kmeans.inertia_)

How Many Clusters?

  • \(W\) always decreases as \(K\) grows, even on test data
  • Look for an “elbow” where the decrease slows down

K-Means on Principal Components

  • Use the first 3 PCs of the ovarian cancer data, ask for 2 clusters
ovarian_pc_scores = ovarian_scores[:, :3]
ovarian_kmeans = KMeans(n_clusters=2, n_init=20, random_state=0).fit(ovarian_pc_scores)

pd.crosstab(ovarian_kmeans.labels_, ovarian_status["status"],
            rownames=["k-means cluster"], colnames=["Diagnosis"])

k-means tips and pitfalls

  • Algorithm not guaranteed to converge
    • Can get wrong answes if nstart too low
    • Can get stuck in local minima
  • Very sensitive to outliers and largest scale of data
    • Always scale data first or used on scaled coordinates
  • Assumes Spherical, Balanced Clusters
  • Will find clusters when there are none
